title: Those using Fable...
author: FapFapNomNom
selftext:
Do you find that its producing better code... or more that its planning out and splitting up high level requests better? I think its (more) the latter... Not that I'm complaining or anything because its quite impressive overall. But its worth dissecting whats really happening here 😉

In other words it feels like a hidden product manager agent has been introduced into the regular dev prompt flow.

comments.author: SanFranLocal
comments.body:
I feel like opus works fine for the level of control I want. I gave fable a big task but it did a bunch of shortcuts I didn't like. 

I do have a plan to try and migrate my iOS game into Unity or more using Fable. I feel like it'll be good at thay

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body:
I had fable work on a MMO version of the classic space game Elite. It did far better than opus would have with less direction. I was particularly impressed with it's ability to adapt our desktop version to be playable on mobile and it's visual reasoning. It's better than opus across the board but the better special awareness and visual reasoning it what really stood out to me.

The game is at https://oort.gg if you want to try it out.

replies.author: HitMePat
replies.body: How are you promoting it to understand spacial reasoning?  Giving it screen shots?

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body: Using playwright so it can test in a browser.

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body: Fable actually started with a full suite of good CRT effects, it decided that was a key partbof the elite experience. I had it remove some of the others for playability but they actually looked pretty good.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Has nothing to do with the splitting up. I already used a complex set of skills and harness to break requests down into bite sized tasks, and I can say definitively that the output and understanding is better. Specifically things like visual/spatial understanding are definitely better, and additionally there is noticeable improvement in simply its understanding of requests (Feels like you don't have to explain things in as much detail and it doesn't get confused / try to take things in different directions randomly.)

That being said, the cost of this seems to be a LOT more tokens and processing. Like the token cost is only supposed to be 2x as much, but it's burning at probably 4x what Opus was. Maybe more tbh. But this could be in part due to some issues with Anthropic's servers because I'm also suddenly having a lot of issues with subagent requests hanging (not even with Fable subagents, but Opus) and slower overall handling of tasks. Overall I'd say you get less results in terms of the value for your token, but it also requires less work from you to get the output you want. So if you value your time more than the money, Fable is the winner. If you are short on $$$ but rich in time, then Fable is not it.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: My first prompt with Fable used 25% of my session limit.  in my next prompt, I began by asking it to be as efficient as possible with token usage while still being effective.  It's output was just as good,  slightly more to the point.  2% usage.  So for me, it's been quite a bit cheaper than opus.

comments.author: RetconnedUsername
comments.body: Yes, it is a massive improvement if you prompt it right.

replies.author: I_Don-t_Care
replies.body: Exactly if you feed it a prompt focused workflow it will not only correctly evaluate what your purpose is from less context, but it will also produce cleaner and simpler code that follows the prompt exactly where it must and with good self-introspection

comments.author: BenTheSodaman
comments.body:
It's ability to plan and see an issue from other perspectives was nice to see + the amount of context it seemed to be retaining over a long session.

Token usage is very high for what it does, relatively speaking.

As it relates to game dev, the end result was a tech demo that would still need a shit load of work to pass muster and was riddled with bugs and UI issues (e.g., keyboard and gamepad focus could move to UI behind the modal windows in the front or messages were displaying out of the viewport and it patted itself on the back after repeated testing / token consumption indicating the messages displayed and were looking good.) 

Some of that could have probably been addressed in the initial prompt and/or patched up with the project rules after, but reiterating, token usage is very high.

2D visuals, audio, and meaningful 3D were about the same / lacking with the default skills it has. You might still get some 3D that looks decently enough for an early 2000s game or a mid-2010s mobile game, but not but gonna need another service to address that side of things to polish it beyond a prompt demo.

comments.author: MysteriousPepper8908
comments.body: I dunno, all I know is that it just does what I ask for without issue. It isn't necessarily the best collaborator, I've found that a lot of its ideas regarding logistics and gameplay are lacking and miss important factors in how the systems come together to produce a satisfying gameplay loop and it pretty much just does what I want how I tell it to do it but if I know what I want, it's unmatched at making it happen with minimal bugs.

comments.author: Aesthetic-Engine
comments.body: I'd been working on a vertical slice but after the stories I heard I decided to tell fable to plan out and take me to beta instead. I'll be there by tomorrow. Excellent model.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
It’s amazing. I throw complex task at it and a few nudges later it’s done. One per phase with a checkin. I had a super complex bug and I did throw 8 fables at it and the went bonkers and solved it. Search online, decompiled some software to verify that solution was the industry standard, planed out the solution implemented it and wrote tests.

That is impressive but the most impressive part is the tool usage. I have a test harness giving the agent human capabilities.  Opus 4.8 was good but fable actually use the tool as I envisioned it.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
My current stage of development is very design heavy, and Fable is definitely better than opus 4.7 and cheaper than 4.8.  I was hitting session limits after an hour or two with opus 4.8.  After prompting Fable to try to be economical with token usage, it was using about 2-4% per prompt.  

I plan to give the design docs these sessions are creating to Fable in Cowork.  Or try to figure out how to get Claudius working for Unreal.  That might be some crazy acceleration.  

Fable working IN editor?  My 5 year plan might become a 1 year plan.

comments.author: samuele_v
comments.body:
To me it feels like Opus is the engaged, enthusiastic middle-ground programmer who knows many facets on many aspects and makes some innocent wrong assumptions about many thing unless you really guide him, but at least he likes keeping you in the loop every step on the way and pumps you up.

Fable is the hikikomori programmer with his own cubicle who receives your instructions, doesn't say anything in return, shuts himself up in his cubicle, you don't hear a sound from the outside, and after 20 minutes he resurfaces and tells you "Done", and it's actually done.

That being said, Fable is better used (in my experience of these 2 days) on complex stuff. Opus can handle the rest just fine.

comments.author: dx0ne
comments.body: Nope. I use orchestration and most code tasks are delegated to Haiku.
